title: Plan and implement interventions and opportunities for transfer of technology

lessons.title: Understanding technology adoption
lessons.html:
What is technology transfer in agriculture?

Technology in agriculture includes new cultivars, improved breeds, conservation agriculture practices, drip irrigation, vaccination programmes, record-keeping apps, post-harvest storage methods and much more. Transfer of technology is the process of moving these innovations from research, industry or other farmers into practical use on farms. The extension practitioner plans and implements interventions that make adoption possible and worthwhile.

How farmers adopt innovations

Adoption is usually a process, not a single event. Farmers typically move through stages:

  1. Awareness: they hear about the technology.
  2. Interest: they seek more information.
  3. Evaluation: they consider whether it suits their situation.
  4. Trial: they test it on a small scale, for example a few rows of a new maize cultivar.
  5. Adoption: they use it fully and continue.

Farmers also adopt at different speeds. A small group of innovators and early adopters try new things quickly; most farmers wait to see results from peers; some adopt late or never. Working with respected early adopters as lead farmers helps spread technology to others.

Factors affecting adoption

FactorQuestion farmers ask
Relative advantageIs it clearly better in yield, income, labour or risk?
CompatibilityDoes it fit my resources, farming system and culture?
ComplexityIs it easy to understand and use?
TrialabilityCan I test it on a small scale first?
ObservabilityCan I see the results on a neighbour's farm?

Beyond the technology itself, adoption depends on access to inputs, credit, markets, labour, information and secure land tenure. A drought-tolerant cultivar is useless if seed is not available locally at planting time. Interventions must address these enabling conditions as well as knowledge.

lessons.title: Planning a technology transfer intervention
lessons.html:
Starting with the farmer's problem

Effective interventions start from a real problem identified with farmers, not from a technology looking for users. For example, communal cattle owners may report high calf losses; the technologies might include improved winter supplementation, vaccination and controlled breeding seasons.

Planning steps

  1. Identify and prioritise the problem with farmers through meetings, farm visits and data such as production records.
  2. Identify suitable technologies from research institutions such as the Agricultural Research Council, universities, commodity organisations and experienced farmers.
  3. Assess fit: check costs, labour, skills, input availability, market demand and risk for the target farmers. Calculate partial budgets in rand to show the expected benefit.
  4. Define the target group and objectives: for example, 30 smallholder maize growers in two villages adopting conservation agriculture on at least one hectare each within two seasons.
  5. Select methods and opportunities: demonstrations, on-farm trials, farmer field schools, farmer days, study tours, mentoring by commercial farmers, and mobile messaging.
  6. Identify partners: input suppliers, researchers, financiers, buyers and local leaders.
  7. Plan resources and schedule: align activities with the farming calendar, budget for inputs, transport and materials, and assign responsibilities.
  8. Plan monitoring and evaluation: decide what will be measured, such as number of farmers trying the technology, yields and income changes.

Creating opportunities for transfer

Opportunities exist beyond formal programmes. Use existing events such as dip days, co-operative meetings, agricultural shows, church gatherings and input supplier open days. Link with government programmes that supply inputs, ensuring that recommended technologies match what is supplied. Partner with private companies who may sponsor demonstrations, while protecting farmers from biased advice.

Plan for risk. A demonstration plot in a drought year may fail. Explain to farmers that results vary with seasons and compare with the conventional practice under the same conditions.

lessons.title: Implementing and evaluating the intervention
lessons.html:
Running demonstrations and trials

On-farm demonstrations are among the most powerful transfer tools because farmers see results under local conditions. To make them effective:

  • Choose a host farmer who is respected, willing and accessible, with a site visible from a road or path.
  • Compare the new practice with the farmer's usual practice side by side, under the same conditions.
  • Agree in writing who supplies inputs, labour and who keeps the harvest.
  • Label plots clearly in the local language.
  • Hold field days at key stages, such as emergence, flowering and harvest, not only at the end.
  • Measure results accurately, for example by weighing harvest from measured areas.

Where chemicals, machinery or animals are involved, include safety in every demonstration: show correct PPE, safe handling and follow the product label. Never encourage farmers to use products outside label instructions.

Supporting adoption after the demonstration

Seeing results is not enough. Farmers need follow-up to apply the technology themselves. Visit early adopters during their first season, solve problems quickly and link them to input suppliers and credit. Encourage lead farmers to share experiences in group meetings. Adapt the technology based on farmer feedback; farmers often find improvements that researchers did not anticipate.

Evaluating the intervention

Measure at different levels:

  1. Activities: number of demonstrations, field days and farmers reached.
  2. Adoption: number and percentage of farmers trying and continuing the technology, and the area or herd size involved.
  3. Results: changes in yield, calving rate, costs, labour and income.
  4. Constraints: reasons farmers did not adopt or stopped using the technology.

Compare with a baseline collected before the intervention. Report results honestly, including failures, to management, partners and researchers. Feedback to researchers is an important part of the extension role, as it improves future technologies.

Key points

  • Adoption passes through awareness, interest, evaluation, trial and adoption.
  • Relative advantage, compatibility, simplicity, trialability and observability drive adoption.
  • Start from a farmer-identified problem and check technical, economic and practical fit.
  • Run side-by-side demonstrations with field days at key stages, and include safety.
  • Follow up adopters, measure against a baseline and feed results back to researchers.
